UNCERTAINTY INLLM AGENTS: A COMPREHENSIVESURVEY Kaiwen Shi1,∗, Zheyuan Zhang1,∗, Caiqi Zhang2, Zheyuan Liu1, Zehong Wang1, Shanglin Wu3,Haoran Wang 3,Kai Shu 3,Han Bao 1,Xiaoyu Ma 4,Yanfang Ye1,† 1University of Notre Dame 2University of Cambridge 3Emory University 4National University of Singapore ∗Equal contribution †Corresponding author ABSTRACT Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents increasingly support consequential decisions and interact with external systems. As these systems move from generating responses to executing actions, however, a confident but unsupported commitment can become a tool call, environmental action, or state update whose effects propagate through later decisions. This risk makes uncertainty essential for characterizing when a model or agent approaches the boundary of reliable commitment. Because uncertainty must ultimately support decisions rather than remain an isolated measurement, this survey organizes the field through a general lifecycle ofQuantification, Calibration, and Utilization. Within this lifecycle, Quantification represents uncertainty-bearing evidence, whereas Calibration relates that evidence to specified reliability outcomes; together, they provide the basis for Utilization, which determines how uncertainty changes inference, action, or learning. This final stage becomes especially consequential in LLM-based agents because each uncertainty-conditioned intervention can reshape the observations, states, and decisions that follow. Accordingly, this survey analyzes agent uncertainty utilization as closed-loop trajectory control across State Construction, Action Selection, Execution & Feedback, and State Update. Along this loop, uncertainty can repair an insufficient decision state, regulate commitment and computational effort, adapt execution to newly observed consequences, and determine which beliefs or learning signals persist. Because an uncertainty signal may be produced at one stage yet consumed at another, existing methods are further organized by signal granularity, uncertainty source stage, and application stage, thereby separating where uncertainty is computed from where it changes agent behavior. This organization, in turn, supports a broader discussion of industrial and consumer deployment, the positive and negative social impacts of uncertainty-aware agents, and open problems in uncertainty propagation, temporal calibration, causal credit assignment, dependence-aware coordination, and intervention-aware evaluation. Overall, this survey shifts attention from estimating uncertainty in isolation to using it to prevent unsupported commitments from propagating through agent trajectories.

PRIME AI paper 1 Introduction Artificial intelligence is expanding the range of cognitive and operational work that can be delegated to machines. Foundation models accelerate this shift by providing a common interface for language, knowledge, perception, computation, and external tools. Large language models are therefore moving beyond answer generation. They increasingly serve as agents that interpret open-ended goals, construct plans, invoke tools, interact with users and environments, and revise later decisions from feedback [1–3]. This transition creates new opportunities in scientific discovery, digital services, embodied systems, and other complex workflows. It also changes the central reliability question. The problem is no longer only whether a model can produce a plausible answer. It is whether an autonomous system can recognize when its current evidence does not support its next action [4–6]. For a standalone language model, an error may remain bounded to an incorrect textual response. For an agent, the same output may become a function call, web operation, GUI action, memory update, or embodied command [4, 6, 7]. Execution changes the external environment. It also changes the evidence available to later decisions. An unsupported commitment can therefore redirect an entire trajectory before terminal failure becomes visible [8–10]. Reliable agency must address this risk before the consequences propagate. The agent must determine whether it should proceed, clarify, retrieve, verify, revise, defer, or delegate [11–13]. This requirement places uncertainty at the foundation of reliable autonomy. In this survey,agent uncertainty concerns whether an agent’s evolving information state provides sufficient support for a current commitment. It also concerns what response should follow when that support is insufficient. This scope is broader than confidence in a completed answer. An agent acts through a sequence of coupled states, actions, observations, and updates. Uncertainty must therefore be interpreted over an evolving decision process [5, 8, 14]. Its value is also behavioral. A signal that identifies fragility but changes neither inference, action, nor learning remains a diagnostic observation. It does not yet function as a mechanism for reliable agency [4, 12, 15]. Research on this problem now spans probabilistic confidence, token-level entropy, sampling-based disagreement, semantic dispersion, verbalized uncertainty, process critics, trajectory-success estimation, calibration, safe planning, recovery, routing, and uncertainty-aware learning [4, 15, 16]. This breadth creates an organizational problem. These methods do not study the same object. A token-level entropy score measures local predictive dispersion. A response-level consistency score measures variation across generations. A calibrated trajectory score estimates a specified reliability outcome. An uncertainty-triggered fallback policy changes what the agent does. All may be described as uncertainty-aware, yet they address different parts of the decision process. A useful survey must therefore connect the signal being measured, the meaning assigned to that signal, and the behavior that consumes it. Existing surveys provide strong foundations for the first parts of this problem. They primarily organize the literature around uncertainty-estimation families, uncertainty sources, model access, computational cost, and calibration quality [17–19]. This estimator-centered view is well suited to the central question of standalone LLM uncertainty: how can uncertainty in a generated output be made observable and evaluated? Recent agent-focused work shows that this question must be extended to underspecified inputs, interactive trajectories, tool use, and communication [1, 16]. However, quantification alone does not cover the full uncertainty problem. An informative signal may carry the wrong reliability meaning. A meaningful signal may still have no effect on behavior. Clarification, retrieval, routing, recovery, and learning are therefore not secondary examples of uncertainty estimation. They are distinct stages in how uncertainty becomes useful. We address this gap by shifting the organizing unit from the uncertainty estimator to the lifecycle of the uncertainty signal. We organize this lifecycle throughQuantification,Calibration, andUtilization.Quantificationmakes insufficient support observable. It represents uncertainty through a score, distribution, set, ranking, semantic variation, internal state, or behavioral proxy [4, 8, 20].Calibrationdetermines what that signal means with respect to a specified reliability event. The event may be response correctness, action reliability, terminal trajectory success, or future success from the current state [9, 15, 21].Utilizationconverts the interpreted signal into an intervention. The intervention may change information acquisition, reasoning, execution, coordination, or learning [7, 11, 12]. The three stages form a dependency chain. Without Quantification, uncertainty remains hidden. Without Calibration, its decision meaning remains unclear. Without Utilization, it cannot 4

Scope and lifecycle (Section 2).Section 2 establishes the conceptual basis of the survey. It first defines uncertainty through the boundary of reliable commitment. Under this view, uncertainty describes whether a model or agent can support an answer, action, reasoning path, tool invocation, or state update under the current condition. The section then distinguishes input, output, and irreducible uncertainty. It also separates uncertainty from confidence, reliability, and trustworthiness. These concepts interact, but they refer to different objects. Confidence represents support for a candidate commitment. Reliability describes dependable system behavior. Trustworthiness includes broader properties such as safety, accountability, and governance. Section 2 finally formalizes the Quantification–Calibration–Utilization lifecycle used throughout the survey. LLM uncertainty quantification (Section 3).Section 3 reviews the uncertainty signals inherited from standalone LLMs. Token-level methods derive uncertainty from predictive probabilities, entropy, divergence, representation distance, density, or mutual information. Response-level methods instead use repeated generations, semantic variation, self-assessment, or evaluator disagreement. These signals form the computational foundation of agent uncertainty because an LLM remains the reasoning and decision backbone of many agents. However, they are defined around individual generations. Section 3 therefore establishes what can be transferred from standalone LLMs before the interaction-specific problems are introduced. Agent uncertainty quantification (Section 4).Section 4 examines what changes when an LLM becomes part of an interactive trajectory. One rollout creates a temporal problem. Local uncertainty may need to be aggregated into a trajectory-level assessment or retained across dependent states. Alternative rollouts create a sampling problem. Uncertainty may then arise from different actions, simulated branches, complete executions, or interacting agents [4, 8, 20]. The section organizes these methods into within-rollout and sampling-based quantification. This separation distinguishes uncertainty inherited from one generation from uncertainty created by sequential interaction. Uncertainty calibration (Section 5).A quantified signal becomes useful only after its reliability target is specified. Section 5 therefore examines how uncertainty is interpreted and corrected. It first reviews testtime and runtime methods that recalibrate existing signals. It then studies training-time methods that teach models to express or preserve calibrated uncertainty. Finally, it considers decision-oriented calibration, where calibration controls the breadth of an agent’s permitted commitment. Agent calibration extends beyond response correctness. It may target action productivity, prefix-conditioned success, terminal trajectory success, or trajectory safety [9, 11, 15, 21]. The section also examines why tool dependence, policy change, delayed feedback, and communication dependence can invalidate a fixed confidence mapping. Uncertainty utilization (Section 6).Once uncertainty has been measured and interpreted, the remaining question is what it changes. Section 6 treats Utilization as the use of uncertainty to alter agent behavior. This literature is highly heterogeneous. Some methods repair missing information. Others control commitment, computation, execution, communication, or learning. Organizing these methods by estimator type would hide these behavioral differences. We therefore introduce a four-stage agent-loop taxonomy that classifies each method by where its uncertainty-conditioned intervention enters the interaction. This taxonomy is a classification device rather than a claim that all agents share one architecture.State Constructioncovers interventions that repair or reorganize instructions, observations, retrieved evidence, memory, and context before commitment.Action Selectioncovers interventions that determine whether the agent should commit, deliberate further, or transfer decision authority.Execution & Feedbackcovers interventions that adapt an ongoing trajectory after tools or environments return new consequences.State Updatecovers interventions that determine which beliefs, memories, communication signals, credit assignments, and policy changes persist into later decisions [5, 12, 22, 23]. This organization separates an uncertainty signal’ssource stagefrom itsapplication stage. It also separates signal granularity from behavioral function. A token-, response-, or trajectory-level signal may support the same intervention, while the same signal may be consumed at several stages. The taxonomy therefore classifies methods by what uncertainty actually changes rather than only by how uncertainty is computed. Domain applications (Section 7).Methods alone do not show where uncertainty has practical value. Section 7 therefore examines domains in which uncertainty changes a consequential decision. Reliable autonomy requires agents not only to act, but also to recognize when their current information does not justify further commitment and to restrict, revise, or transfer that commitment before its consequences propagate. 2 The Scope of Uncertainty Conceptual clarity is necessary because uncertainty is often used together with confidence, trustworthiness, reliability, calibration, and robustness, even though these concepts refer to different objects and levels of analysis. Without a clear scope, uncertainty may be reduced to a confidence score, or confused with system-level trustworthiness. We therefore first position uncertainty relative to the classical aleatoric–epistemic distinction, then formalize it as a model-centered relation to the boundary of reliable commitment. We further distinguish uncertainty from related concepts and introduce the lifecycle view of quantification, calibration, and utilization. 2.1 Uncertainty: Towards the boundary of reliable commitment In classical machine learning, uncertainty is commonly decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty and epistemic uncertainty. The former arises from irreducible randomness or ambiguity in the data-generating process, while the latter reflects the learner’s lack of knowledge and can in principle be reduced by additional information [159]. Recent surveys on LLM uncertainty often inherit this distinction and adapt it to language generation [17–19]. This view remains useful, however, in the era of LLMs and agents, the scope of uncertainty needs to be calibrated to the behaviors these systems actually perform. Because the relevant question is often not only what the model knows, but what the model can responsibly treat as sufficiently supported. Recent work has therefore discussed uncertainty in relation to input ambiguity, reasoning divergence, decoding variability, semantic variation, tool interaction, and long-horizon trajectories [16, 18, 84]. These developments do not invalidate the classical aleatoric–epistemic distinction. Rather, they suggest that aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty should be treated as source-level categories, while the conceptual scope of uncertainty should be extended from fixed predictions to the broader commitments made by LLMs and agents. Therefore, in this paper, we define uncertainty asa measure of the boundary of reliable commitment, which characterizes the degree to which a model approaches the limit of what it can reliably predict, infer, explain, decide, or act upon under a given condition. 6

PRIME AI paper Definition: Boundary of Reliable Commitment.Formally, letMdenote a model and letxdenote the condition faced by the model. We defineC M(x)as the space of possible commitments thatMmay make underx, where eachc∈ C M(x)may correspond to an answer, an action, a reasoning path, a tool invocation, or a state update. Within this space, the model has a reliable-commitment region: RM(x) ={c∈ C M(x) :Mcan reliably commit tocunderx}. The boundary of reliable commitment is the frontier of this region: BM(x) =∂R M(x). With this boundary formalized, uncertainty describes the model’s relation to this boundary. It is high when a commitment is close to the frontier between what the model can reliably commit to and what it cannot. It is low when the commitment lies well inside the reliable-commitment region. Under this definition, uncertainty can be further organized by whether the source lies primarily in the task condition or in the model’s commitment. •Input uncertainty.Input uncertainty arises when the conditionxis ambiguous, incomplete, underspecified, or conflicting. In this case, the model may be uncertain not because it lacks the ability to solve the task, but because the available condition does not support a unique reliable commitment. Such uncertainty can often be reduced through interaction, such as asking clarification questions, retrieving additional evidence, or obtaining new observations. •Output uncertainty.Output uncertainty arises when the model cannot reliably support a commitment even under the given condition. This uncertainty reflects limitations in the model’s knowledge, reasoning ability, tool-use competence, or behavioral stability. Unlike input uncertainty, it cannot be fully resolved by merely clarifying the input; it requires stronger model competence, better evidence integration, improved reasoning, or external verification. •Irreducible uncertaintyarises when the condition and the model are both insufficient to determine a single certain outcome because the underlying process is inherently variable or only partially observable. This uncertainty cannot be fully eliminated by clarification or model improvement. It can only be represented, calibrated, and managed when making downstream decisions. For LLMs and agents, this distinction is useful because uncertainty may come either from an unclear task condition or from the model’s inability to make a reliable answer, action, tool invocation, or state update. Moreover, a commitment is broader than a final prediction.It refers to any answer, reasoning step, tool use, state description, or decision that the model treats as sufficiently supported. This broader scope allows uncertainty to cover both traditional prediction uncertainty and the additional uncertainty sources discussed for LLMs and agents [17–19]. Under this view, a condition is low-uncertainty for a model when the model has enough knowledge, reasoning ability, or tool-use competence to support a stable commitment. When uncertainty is high, the model’s behavior suggests that multiple commitments remain plausible, or that its current commitment is close to the boundary beyond which it can no longer be treated as reliable. 2.2 Conceptual Boundaries of Uncertainty In the literature on LLMs and agents, terms such as confidence, uncertainty, trustworthiness, and reliability are often used together, and sometimes even interchangeably. Therefore, before proceeding, we clarify several concepts that are closely related to uncertainty but should not be treated as equivalent to it, which helps delimit the scope of our survey. •Confidence: A Candidate-Level Representation of Uncertainty.Confidence is closely related to uncertainty, but it is usually a positive score attached to a specific candidate, such as a predicted label, answer, action, or hypothesis. When the prediction target is fixed and the confidence score is tied to a particular class probability, well-calibrated confidence can serve as a useful uncertainty estimate, especially in 8

PRIME AI paper simple classification settings. However, the distinction becomes necessary when the object of uncertainty is broader than a specified candidate. A model may report confidence in a particular answer, while the relevant uncertainty concerns whether the model knows the answer at all, whether the answer is stable, or whether the model is operating within its reliable competence boundary. Intuitively, confidence asks how strongly the model supports one candidate, while uncertainty asks whether the model has enough knowledge to make a reliable commitment [160]. Accordingly, confidence is best understood as one operational representation of uncertainty, while uncertainty itself remains the broader concept that organizes what these representations are trying to measure. •Trustworthiness: A Multidimensional Socio-Technical Objective.Trustworthiness is a multidimensional system-level and socio-technical property of AI systems [161–163]. Calibration is not any method that computes uncertainty or improves agent reliability. The target and granularity of this relation must therefore be stated explicitly. Elicitation exposes an uncertainty signal, while diagnosis tests whether that signal already tracks the intended event; neither operation corrects the relation by itself. Post-hoc calibration learns a fixed correction, runtime calibration updates that correction from deployment feedback, and training-time calibration builds the alignment into the learned model. By contrast, using uncertainty only to select samples, allocate credit, regulate exploration, or weight experience does not constitute calibration unless the objective also aligns the signal with a defined reliability target. A single system may contain several of these operations, so classification should occur at the mechanism level rather than the paper level. Decision-oriented conformal methods remain within calibration because they use calibration data to convert a score into a statistically controlled coverage or risk boundary. Under this definition, calibration answers one precise question: how reliably does an uncertainty signal represent the event it is claimed to predict? 6 Uncertainty Utilization in LLM-Based Agents: Turning Uncertainty into Adaptive Behavior Uncertainty utilization begins when an uncertainty signal changes system behavior. Quantification makes uncertainty observable, while calibration aligns the signal with a defined reliability event. Neither step alone determines what the system should do next [11, 12]. In standalone LLMs, utilization usually remains local to one generation. It determines whether the model answers or abstains, which candidates it retains, how it revises the current response, or how response-level behavior is optimized [107, 114, 121]. Agents extend this role across the full interaction loop. During State Construction, uncertainty identifies when the decision context is incomplete or unreliable. Clarification supplies missing intent or task constraints. Value-aware information acquisition selects the question or source expected to reduce decision-relevant uncertainty most. Context reorganization filters, re-ranks, or restructures evidence that is already available but poorly represented [22, 124, 127]. During Action Selection, uncertainty controls whether and how the agent commits. Retrieval supplies evidence that is still missing. Abstention or termination blocks a commitment that remains unsupported. Deliberation assigns more reasoning, sampling, or verification to contested decisions. Comparative routing transfers authority to a model or agent judged more reliable for the current choice [13, 104, 140]. During Execution & Feedback, uncertainty responds to consequences that become visible only after an action or simulation. Local expansion reopens an unstable transition and generates alternative continuations from that point. Rollout budget allocation divides a fixed sampling budget between complete trajectories and local branches. Search adaptation uses returned outcomes to expand promising branches, prune weak ones, backtrack, or regenerate an action. Recovery repairs a localized failure, while termination stops execution when further attempts are unlikely to justify their cost [3, 5, 137]. During State Update, uncertainty determines which information and experience influence later decisions. Belief and memory revision weakens, corrects, or replaces unsupported claims. Confidence-weighted communication controls how strongly messages from other agents enter the shared state. Delayed credit assignment maps a final outcome back to the earlier decisions that should receive learning pressure. Uncertainty-shaped rewards and exploration then determine which behaviors the updated policy reinforces, suppresses, or preserves [23, 82, 157]. These methods are classified by the intervention they execute rather than by the estimator they use. A signal may be produced at one stage and consumed at another, so its source stage and application stage must remain separate. This organization treats agent uncertainty utilization as closed-loop trajectory control rather than output-local uncertainty handling. 25

Classification should follow this direct intervention rather than the estimator that produces the signal. Accordingly, this section compares applications along four dimensions: the commitment at stake, the uncertainty that determines whether the commitment is supported, the intervention triggered when support is insufficient, and the evidence that the intervention improves the relevant outcome. This decision-centered view separates the operational use of uncertainty from the mere reporting of confidence and provides a common basis for examining AI4Science, healthcare, VLA and robotics, and software and web agents. The maturity of the evidence, however, differs across these domains. AI4Science, healthcare, and robotics inherit established traditions in predictive uncertainty quantification, active learning, and classical decision making, but much of this work stops before uncertainty enters a sequential autonomous loop. AI4Science selects experiments and determines whether evidence licenses a scientific claim. Healthcare decides whether a case remains automated or moves to professional oversight. VLA and robotics decide whether multimodal evidence supports physical action. Software and web agents decide 41

Scientific systems face uncertainty over hypotheses, designs, measurements, and inferences. Clinical systems face uncertainty over case applicability and evidence sufficiency. VLA and robotic systems face uncertainty across perception, grounding, planning, and execution. Software and web agents face uncertainty over task specifications, context, candidate actions, and verification evidence. Application value is demonstrated by the intervention, not by the uncertainty score alone.Across domains, uncertainty can select an experiment, acquire another measurement, abstain from a diagnosis, request a specialist, look again, re-ground an object, revise a plan, clarify a software requirement, strengthen a test, or transfer control. The strongest evidence for an uncertainty application is therefore a demonstrated change in a consequential decision. Evaluation must then test whether that change improves the relevant trade-off among task success, information gain, risk, resource cost, delay, unnecessary intervention, and harm. It must also distinguish mature domain-level uncertainty estimation from agent-level uncertainty use. A calibrated predictor does not by itself establish that an autonomous system can recognize insufficient support and respond before the resulting commitment becomes consequential. 8 Open Problems The open problems below do not ask which additional technique should be introduced. Instead, they question assumptions that have emerged as agent uncertainty research has become increasingly fine-grained, calibrated, and behavior-oriented. In each case, the literature has established that a more sophisticated uncertainty mechanism can be constructed, but has not yet established whether that added sophistication materially improves agent decisions or outcomes. We therefore formulate each problem as a direct question whose answer could confirm, limit, or redirect an existing line of research. 8.1 Quantification: Which Uncertainty Representations Are Actually Necessary? Is Turn-Level Uncertainty Necessary for Multi-Turn Agents?Research on trajectory uncertainty has moved from assigning confidence only to the final answer, to estimating uncertainty at individual turns, and then to aggregating or propagating these local estimates across the full trajectory. This progression implicitly assumes that uncertainty attached to each thought, action, or observation provides information that cannot be recovered from the trajectory as a whole. However, a holistic estimator conditioned on the complete interaction history may already predict eventual success without assigning a separate uncertainty value to every intermediate turn. Turn-level estimation also introduces additional computation, noisy local signals, and difficult choices about how those signals should be combined or propagated. At the same time, a single trajectory-level score may reveal that the overall process is risky without showing when the risk emerged or whether the agent still had an opportunity to respond. The fundamental question therefore comes before the design of better propagation methods:does turn-level uncertainty provide a practical capability that trajectory-level uncertainty cannot provide, or does it mainly add complexity to a problem that can be solved holistically? Does Finer-Grained Uncertainty Actually Improve Agent Decisions?Uncertainty quantification has progressively decomposed a generic confidence score into uncertainty over user specifications, tool choices, function arguments, assumptions, actions, and plans. This decomposition is intuitively attractive because an agent does not merely generate text; it commits to structured decisions whose individual components may fail for different reasons. Nevertheless, identifying which field is uncertain does not automatically tell the agent whether the complete commitment is reliable. The risk of a tool invocation may depend jointly on the recipient, account, amount, permission, and operation type, while the consequence of the action may matter more than the uncertainty of any one field. Increasing granularity may therefore produce a more detailed description of fragility without changing the eventual decision to execute, verify, or abstain. It may also introduce additional estimation and calibration errors at every decomposed level.How much structure must uncertainty represent before it becomes genuinely actionable, and at what point does further decomposition become descriptive complexity without measurable reliability gains? When Does Multi-Agent Agreement Reduce Uncertainty Rather Than Amplify Shared Error?Multiagent uncertainty research has developed from measuring disagreement among final answers to examining 42

PRIME AI paper reasoning alignment, communication dependence, interaction dynamics, and system-level confidence. This development exposes a basic assumption behind multi-agent systems: adding more agents is useful only when they contribute sufficiently independent evidence or reasoning. Agents may agree because they reached the same conclusion independently, but they may also agree because they share the same foundation model, retriever, prompt, memory, training data, or upstream tool error. Communication can further synchronize initially different agents, creating consensus by spreading one mistake through the group. Under these conditions, adding agents may reduce measured disagreement while leaving actual reliability unchanged or even making the shared error harder to challenge. Calibrating each agent separately does not resolve this problem if their failures remain correlated after composition.Under what conditions does multi-agent agreement constitute genuinely new evidence, and when is apparent consensus only a repeated or communication-amplified version of the same uncertainty? 8.2 Calibration: When Does Better Calibration Matter for Decisions? Must Uncertainty Be Calibrated at Every Turn?Calibration research has moved from evaluating one terminal confidence score to assigning probability-like meaning to the entire confidence process produced throughout a trajectory. A complete calibrated trace appears stronger because it describes how confidence evolves as the agent reasons, acts, and observes new information. Yet it remains unclear whether every intermediate estimate needs to be calibrated with equal precision. Many turns are internal, reversible, or behaviorally inconsequential, and calibration errors at those turns may never affect an external decision. A process-level metric can therefore reward accurate probabilities at numerous unimportant steps while obscuring whether confidence was reliable at the few moments when the agent committed to an action, selected a tool, or decided not to seek help. Conversely, calibrating only the final score may detect miscalibration after the opportunity to change behavior has already passed.Does calibrating the full uncertainty trace materially improve agent control, or is reliable calibration needed only at the consequential decision points where a different confidence value could still change the trajectory? Can Runtime Calibration Be Evaluated When Its Own Interventions Hide Errors?Calibration has increasingly shifted from one-time offline correction toward runtime adaptation because confidence semantics change across tasks, users, tools, models, and deployment environments. However, an uncertainty-aware agent does not passively observe deployment outcomes; its own confidence determines which outcomes are allowed to occur. Low-confidence cases may be interrupted, deferred to a stronger model, handed to a human, or abandoned before completion, while high-confidence cases remain under autonomous execution. The resulting feedback is therefore selective: the system observes outcomes for the cases it chose to handle, but often never observes what would have happened on the cases it removed. This creates the possibility of selfconfirming calibration. A system may appear increasingly well calibrated simply because its most difficult cases are no longer included in the observed evaluation set, rather than because its probability estimates have become more reliable.Can runtime calibration be meaningfully validated when uncertainty-based intervention changes which outcomes are observed and conceals precisely the failures needed to test whether the calibration remains correct? Do Better Calibration Metrics Actually Improve Agent Success?Agent uncertainty research has devoted substantial effort to reducing metrics such as ECE, Brier score, and related response- or trajectory-level calibration errors. These metrics are useful for evaluating whether reported probabilities correspond to empirical outcomes, but their improvement is often treated as evidence that the agent itself has become more reliable. That implication is not guaranteed. Agent control usually depends on whether confidence changes a concrete decision near a threshold: whether to continue, retrieve, verify, defer, or stop. A substantial improvement in average calibration error may leave all of these decisions unchanged, producing no improvement in task success, safety, or resource allocation. Conversely, a model with slightly worse global calibration may be more accurate around the particular boundary that determines intervention and may therefore achieve better outcomes. It is possible that calibration only needs to be sufficiently accurate for the relevant control decision, after which further optimization of numerical calibration metrics offers little practical value.How much calibration is enough, and when do further gains in calibration metrics stop translating into meaningful gains in agent success or control? 43

PRIME AI paper 8.3 Utilization: Does Uncertainty Lead to the Right Behavior? Does Clarification Resolve Uncertainty or Transfer It to the User?Clarification research has progressed from detecting underspecified requests to deciding when an agent should ask and which missing information a question should target. This development treats clarification as a deliberate uncertainty-reduction mechanism rather than a generic conversational behavior. However, asking a question does not guarantee that uncertainty is removed. The user may also be uncertain, may misunderstand the question, may provide an incomplete or inconsistent answer, or may revise a preference after the agent has already acted on earlier information. Additional questions can also increase interaction burden, enlarge the context, interrupt an otherwise recoverable workflow, and create new opportunities for misunderstanding. An agent may therefore become more active in asking questions without becoming more successful at completing the underlying task. Clarification can even make uncertainty less visible by replacing an explicit ambiguity with an answer that appears definite but is unreliable.When does clarification genuinely reduce uncertainty relevant to the next decision, and when does it merely move that uncertainty from the agent to the user or hide it behind additional interaction? Does Retrieval Add Reliable Evidence or Merely Increase Confidence?Uncertainty-guided retrieval has developed from a binary decision about whether to search toward controlling search depth, retries, stopping, and evidence sufficiency. This progression assumes that additional retrieval can reduce uncertainty by providing information unavailable to the model. Yet retrieved information may be noisy, contradictory, redundant, outdated, or derived from the same underlying source. Multiple documents can therefore appear to provide independent support while merely repeating one unsupported claim. Language models may also become more confident because retrieved text is detailed or persuasive, even when it does not establish the conclusion required for the task. This creates a particularly dangerous interaction when confidence is also used as the stopping signal: unreliable evidence may increase confidence and cause the agent to terminate the search precisely when further verification is most needed.How can we determine whether retrieval has actually reduced epistemic uncertainty by adding reliable evidence, rather than simply increasing the agent’s subjective confidence in a conclusion that remains unsupported? Can Uncertainty Alone Identify the Right Intervention?Uncertainty is now used to trigger additional reasoning, resampling, retrieval, clarification, verification, retry, deferral, and abstention. Existing studies show that uncertainty can improve each of these mechanisms when the available intervention is specified in advance. A clarification method assumes that uncertainty should lead to a question; a retrieval method assumes that it should lead to search; a deferral method assumes that it should lead to a stronger model. These results establish that uncertainty can determinewhento activate a particular mechanism, but not that it can determine whichmechanism is appropriate. The same uncertainty value may arise because information is missing, reasoning is unstable, a tool has failed, available evidence is contradictory, or the task lies outside the agent’s competence. These cases may require fundamentally different responses, and applying the wrong intervention can waste computation, introduce further noise, or reinforce the original error.Does an uncertainty signal contain enough information to identify the appropriate response, or does current uncertainty-guided control confuse detecting fragility with diagnosing what should be done about it? Across these problems, the common unresolved assumption is that more detailed uncertainty representations, lower calibration error, and more uncertainty-driven behavior will naturally produce more reliable agents. The development of the field has shown that each of these improvements is technically possible, but it has not yet established where they provide indispensable decision value and where they merely produce richer descriptions, better-looking metrics, or more elaborate control mechanisms. The central research question is therefore not simply whether uncertainty can be estimated more precisely, but whether that precision changes agent behavior in a way that consistently improves the final outcome. 44
